Feature Documentary  —  90 Minutes
THE SCOUT & THE SCHOLAR
Two men who couldn’t have been more different built the most important partnership in the history of basketball. This is the story nobody told while they were alive.

Feature Documentary

The Film

For forty years, Garf and Tom shaped the game. More than fifty Hall of Famers passed through their hands. They never took a check from a shoe company, never sold a kid short, never forgot a face. Then they both died. And the men who loved them realized the story had never been told.

Why This Film, Why Now

The Last People Who Knew

Every year, more coaches who remember Garf and Tom retire. Every year, the living archive shrinks. The players they discovered are in their fifties now. Some of them are gone too.

The sport they gave their lives to has changed beyond recognition. AAU circuits run on shoe money. Recruiting is a business with agents and NIL deals before a kid turns sixteen. The thing Garf and Tom refused to compromise was the opposite of all of that: seeing a player clearly, honestly, and without an agenda was the whole job. That it was also a moral act.

This film makes that argument. Not with nostalgia. With evidence.

Carnegie Deli, 854 Seventh Avenue. His table was in the back.
Our Guide

Barry “Slice” Rohrssen

Slice was a college coach for thirty years. He was Garf’s friend, Tom’s friend, and the man who was present when each of them died. He is not a disinterested narrator. He is a man on a mission.

He will travel the country asking the people whose lives Garf and Tom changed to tell him what they remember. The question underneath all of it is simpler: what do we lose when men like this are gone?

The film owes something to Citizen Kane and Searching for Sugar Man: a devoted believer reconstructing a life through the testimony of people transformed by it. But Slice already knows the answer. The journey is about making sure the record is complete.

Queens, August 2023. Tom still had his notebook.
Our Two Subjects
01  —  The Scout
Howard “Garf” Garfinkel
Born the Bronx, 1929. Died New York, 2016.

Garf was a Damon Runyon character who wandered into the wrong century and decided it was fine. Loud, funny, cigar in hand, no filter. He co-founded High School Basketball Illustrated in 1965 and ran Five-Star Basketball Camp from 1966 to 2008. His gift was not analysis; it was instinct. He knew a player the way a great poker player knows a hand.

Inducted into the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame in 2021, five years after he died.

02  —  The Scholar
Tom Konchalski
Born Manhattan, 1947. Died Queens, 2021.

Tom graduated magna cum laude from Fordham. He never owned a car. He rode the subway to every game he scouted for fifty years and never accepted a free meal from a college coach. His reports evaluated players on thirteen criteria including SAT scores. Coaches called him the conscience of recruiting. He went to Mass every morning.

Inducted into the National Collegiate Basketball Hall of Fame in 2023. Not yet in Springfield. Many people believe this is an injustice. This film agrees.

On tone: This film is not an elegy. Garf was the funniest person in every room he ever entered. Tom had a scholar’s dry wit and a Jesuit’s patience. The film earns the right to its serious argument by spending a good amount of time laughing. It should feel like a great dinner with people who have nothing left to prove.

Five-Star Basketball Camp. The proving ground Garf built from nothing in 1966.
Structure and Scenes

More than a conventional timeline, this film is built from scenes — verité moments, anchor sequences, and interview encounters that accumulate into an argument about what basketball lost, and what it cost.

01
Act One
The Handshake
We establish the world, the two men, and the question that drives the film. The audience learns who Garf and Tom were, and why the people who knew them refuse to stop talking about them.
Anchor Scene
The Storage Unit

Slice opens Tom’s storage unit. Nobody has been inside since Tom died. Notebooks, scouting reports, correspondence, a typewriter — the physical record of fifty years of watching basketball with complete attention and zero agenda. The scene does not editorialize. It lets the objects speak.

The Throughline Begins
Slice and the Deli

Slice stands outside the closed Carnegie Deli on Seventh Avenue. Garf’s table was in the back. The deli closed December 2016, seven months after Garf died. He has talked, in idle moments, about what it would take to bring it back for one day — the coaches, the players, Garf’s people gathered at Garf’s table. It may never happen. But the idea runs through the film as a kind of horizon.

Two Portraits
The Odd Couple

Garf’s world: the deli, the cigar, the blacktop, the phone that never stopped ringing. Tom’s world: Mass at 7am, the subway, Fordham, the notebook, the typewriter. Tom’s audio recordings surface here for the first time, including “Who the F**k is Mike Jordan,” in his own voice.

Running Thread
The Graves

Slice visits the graves of Garf and Tom, ideally on a birthday or a death anniversary. He doesn’t say much. He doesn’t need to. It establishes what kind of man he is and what kind of film this is going to be.

Act Two  —  The Proving Ground
The Stories.

The famous ones and the ones nobody knows. A Hall of Famer’s testimony carries no more weight here than a city council member from Newark saying the same thing. Coaches and players alike — the men whose lives were shaped by what Garf and Tom saw in them.

Before the logo. Before the commercials. Before anyone knew his name.
The World They Built
Five-Star

Garf built Five-Star Basketball Camp in 1966 with no money and a mailing list. By the 1980s it was the most important summer program in American basketball. No pay-to-play, no shortcut. The camp is how Garf built his credibility and how Tom built his relationships. And it is where coaches first understood what it meant to have these two men watching.

The Must-Tell Story
Who the F**k is Mike Jordan

Tom recorded this story himself, on audio, in his own words. A kid from Wilmington arrived at Five-Star and worked in the cafeteria to pay his way in — but he played too, and that summer he was the best player on the court. Garf saw him. Tom saw him. They did not need to discuss it. What followed put Michael Jordan in front of Dean Smith. The rest is not the story. This is the story.

Anchor Scene
Slice Courtside

Slice at a game, ideally a college game in a gym that looks like the gyms Garf and Tom worked. Walking the arena before tip-off, sitting with someone who knew them. The conversation that happens naturally in that setting is the conversation the film has been building toward.

The Interviews
The People Who Remember

Coaches, players, and others on camera with Slice present and active. The cinematic approach will emphasize creative angles that make both interviewer and interviewee active characters, refusing the standard talking-head format. Famous names matter, and so do the men no headline ever mentioned.

Act Three  —  The Legacy

The Reckoning.

The sport Garf and Tom gave their lives to has changed beyond recognition. AAU circuits run on shoe money. Recruiting operates with agents and NIL deals before a kid turns seventeen. Analytics dashboards have replaced the legal pad. The human being in front of you — his character, his family, the way he treats a teammate after a turnover — does not show up in the data.

The film does not make this argument with nostalgia. It makes it with evidence. Coach after coach, unprompted, says the same thing: there will never be others like them. That is not sentiment. It is a diagnosis. Something specific was lost when Garf and Tom died, and the sport has not found a way to replace it. Sonny Vaccaro — who built the shoe money world from the other side — is the right person to name what that is.

The Central Argument
What No Machine Can Do

Tom’s reports evaluated players on thirteen criteria, including character and academic record. He watched a player the way a confessor listens: completely, without agenda, looking for what was true. Garf’s gift was different, felt rather than analyzed. The sport now has biometric data and AI scouting tools. None of it does what Tom did on a wooden bleacher with a legal pad, because what Tom was doing was not analysis. He was paying attention.

The Unfinished Business
Springfield

Garf went into the Naismith Hall in 2021, five years after he died. Tom went into the National Collegiate Hall in 2023. He is not yet in Springfield. The coaches and players who say, on camera, that this is an injustice are not a small group. The film does not editorialize. It lets them make the case.

Anchor Scene / Resolution
The Deli

The finale, if it happens: that room full of people. Coaches, players, the men from Newark and the Bronx, people whose names are on arena facades and people whose names are on nothing. All of them in Garf’s place, at Garf’s table, because Slice asked them to come. It is not a celebration. It is a completion.

Final Scene
The Notebook

Slice sits with the notebooks. Eleven thousand pages of handwritten scouting reports. He reads one aloud: a player from 1987, a small school, a kid nobody else was watching. Tom had seen something. The camera holds on the handwriting. The film ends without a verdict, because the verdict is already in the room.

Why This Approach

A Story for Now, Not Then

The trap with a film like this is nostalgia. Two beloved men who are gone, a sport that has changed, coaches who shake their heads. We have been careful not to make that film. Nostalgia is comfortable, and it is useless. What Garf and Tom built was not just admirable in its time — it is a direct challenge to how basketball operates right now, in this recruiting cycle, in this transfer portal, with these shoe deals and these algorithms. The film is in conversation with the present at every turn.

The question is not what we lost. The question is whether anyone is willing to say what we lost and why it matters — and then make the case that it can be recovered.

Slice is not a narrator. He is the argument in motion. He is a man who learned from Garf and Tom, who coached under Calipari and Mullin, who has seen the sport from both sides of the recruiting table. When he sits across from a coach and asks what Tom meant to him, he is not gathering testimony for a memorial. He is building a case. His grief is real and it is present, but it has somewhere to go: he wants to change something, or at least to make someone feel the weight of what changed without anyone noticing.

That urgency is what separates this film from a tribute. The coaches and players we are interviewing are not speaking about history. They are speaking about a standard that still exists in their memory, a standard that the sport has quietly abandoned, and a standard that they would restore if they knew how. The film holds that contradiction honestly. It does not pretend the clock can be turned back. It does insist that the values Garf and Tom embodied — seeing the human being in front of you, telling the truth about what you see, refusing to let money buy your judgment — are not obsolete. They are just unfashionable. There is a difference.

We want an audience that loves basketball to leave this film thinking differently about what the sport costs the people inside it. And we want an audience that has never watched a game to leave having met two men they wish they had known. Both of those audiences exist. This film is for both of them.
